title: How Retrieval Practice Changed My Teaching
author: Science of Reading Classroom
summary: This first-person reflection describes how participation in a teaching fellowship's Science of Learning curriculum prompted an experienced teacher to immediately shift toward evidence-based retrieval practice — and how the impact spread across a grade-level team, a school newsletter, a Teaching and Learning Summit, and a public TableTalk. The author's central admission is that despite years of experience and familiarity with research, she was not consistently applying the highest-leverage strategies for how the brain actually learns, and that a single Sunday-evening fellowship meeting changed her classroom the next morning. Retrieval practice proved immediately implementable without new materials or extended training: brain dumps, retrieval grids, and intentional turn-and-talks with accountability structures could be layered into existing curriculum at the point where she chose to ask rather than tell. Positive retention effects appeared almost immediately, with learning consolidating in long-term memory in ways the author could observe within days. The article's core appeal is accessibility: the barrier to entry for high-impact retrieval strategies is essentially zero, making widespread adoption a question of professional will rather than resource constraint, and suggesting that the gap between knowing research and applying it is itself the central professional development problem to solve.
points: Retrieval practice requires no new materials, no extended training, and no preparation time beyond identifying the moments in an existing lesson where 'stop telling and start asking' applies — the implementation cost is essentially zero relative to the learning impact.

The shift from teacher-summarising to student-retrieving is a single deliberate instructional decision: replacing 'let me remind you' with 'pull out what you know' changes how the brain processes and consolidates content, with measurable effects appearing within days.

The article implicitly diagnoses a professional culture problem: experienced teachers know research but are not systematically applying it, suggesting that the gap between professional knowledge and classroom practice is the primary problem retrieval practice proponents need to address.

Sharing evidence-based strategies across a team and at school-wide professional development generates disproportionate impact: the author's classroom shift eventually reached a Teaching and Learning Summit and a public TableTalk, multiplying individual adoption into institutional practice.
quotes: Our first month centered around the Science of Learning, specifically on retrieval practice. I sat there listening, thinking to myself, This is so seemingly obvious, easy to implement, and high impact… so why wasn't I doing it?

I realized that despite all my experience and knowledge, I wasn't consistently using the best evidence-based practices to support how the brain actually learns. And I decided to change that the very next day.

The next morning, I looked at my curriculum and identified moments where I could stop telling and start asking. Some of this even just came to me on the spot. Instead of me standing at the front summarizing what we learned yesterday, I asked them to pull that information out of their own heads.
Positive effects started occurring almost immediately. Learning was sticking in long term memory.

It took me back to one of my favorite college courses—The Psychology of Learning. It all felt so full circle. This is how science has proven the brain learns best. When you realize how low the barrier to entry is for these strategies, it makes you wonder why we aren't all teaching this way by default.

The feedback from other teachers was the most rewarding part. They loved that it wasn't another 'overwhelming PD' full of things we don't have the time or capacity to actually do. It was just real, manageable changes that actually work.

Seeing the impact in my own classroom has been a game-changer. It's a reminder that we don't always need to reinvent the wheel; evidence based practices exist for a reason, and sometimes the tiniest change can make the biggest difference.
